title: Sales Ledger Control Account: Meaning and Structure
summary: What control accounts are, why they are used, and the items on the debit and credit sides of the sales ledger control account.

p: A control account is a summary account that shows the total of a group of individual accounts in one account. It is also called a total account. There are two kinds: the sales ledger control account (the total debtors account) and the purchases ledger control account (the total creditors account).

The sales ledger control account shows the total of all the individual debtors' accounts in the sales ledger. It is also called the total debtors account, the debtors control account or the receivables control account.

1. Quick information: the total owed by all customers is available at once, without adding hundreds of accounts. 2. To detect errors: the control account balance is compared with the total of the individual balances; if they differ, there is an error. 3. Division of work: one person keeps the control account and another keeps the individual accounts, which reduces the risk of fraud. 4. To save time when extracting a trial balance: only the control account balance is needed. 5. As an internal check on the ledger clerks. 6. To locate errors quickly, because they are limited to one section. 7. To give management summary figures.

sections.h: Structure of the sales ledger control account
p: Because debtors are assets, the account has a debit balance. Debit side: things that INCREASE what customers owe. Credit side: things that DECREASE it.

head: Debit side (increases debtors)
Credit side (decreases debtors)
rows: Cash and bank received from debtors
Credit sales (total of the sales day book)
Closing balance c/d (debtors at the end)

p: Opening balance: the total owed by customers at the start of the period. Credit sales: only sales on credit, from the sales day book; cash sales are NOT included because they do not create debtors. Dishonoured cheques: a cheque from a customer that was banked but returned unpaid; the customer still owes the money. Interest charged: a penalty for late payment, which increases the debt.

Cash or bank received: the money received from customers, from the cash book. Returns inwards: goods the customers sent back, from the returns inwards day book. Discount allowed: cash discount given for prompt payment. Bad debts written off: debts confirmed as irrecoverable, from the journal. Contra: when the same person is both a debtor and a creditor, the smaller amount is set off. Example: a customer owes us ₦10,000 and we owe him ₦4,000; the contra is ₦4,000.
Memory aid: ask 'does this increase what customers owe us?' If yes, it is a debit. If it reduces what they owe, it is a credit.

title: Preparing a Sales Ledger Control Account and Reconciling It
summary: Worked examples of the sales ledger control account, how to reconcile it with the individual debtors' balances, and causes of differences.

p: Debtors at 1 January ₦80,000; credit sales ₦150,000; cash received from debtors ₦120,000; returns inwards ₦8,000; discount allowed ₦5,000; bad debts written off ₦3,000.

Opening ₦80,000 + credit sales ₦150,000 = ₦230,000. Less cash 120,000, returns 8,000, discount 5,000 and bad debts 3,000 = ₦136,000. Closing balance = ₦94,000. The customers owe ₦94,000 at the end of January.

Debtors at 1 June ₦120,000; credit sales ₦280,000; cash sales ₦150,000; cash received from debtors ₦240,000; cheques received from debtors ₦60,000; returns inwards ₦15,000; discount allowed ₦12,000; bad debts ₦8,000; dishonoured cheque ₦5,000; interest charged ₦2,000; contra with creditors ₦4,000.

The cash sales of ₦150,000 are NOT included because they do not make debtors. Cash and cheques received are both money from debtors and can be shown as one figure of ₦300,000. The dishonoured cheque and the interest go on the debit side because they increase the debt. The contra goes on the credit side because it reduces the debt. The closing balance of ₦68,000 is the total owed by all customers.
Step 1: take the control account balance. Step 2: list and add up the individual debtors' balances from the sales ledger. Step 3: compare them. Step 4: if they differ, find and correct the error.
Example: control account ₦94,000. Individual balances: A 30,000; B 25,000; C 20,000; D 19,000 = ₦94,000. They agree.

Example with an error: control ₦94,000 and individual total ₦97,000, a difference of ₦3,000. The cause: a bad debt of ₦3,000 was written off in the control account but not in the individual debtor's account. Write it off there too and the total becomes ₦94,000.

An error in adding the sales day book; a credit sale posted to the wrong debtor (this affects the individual accounts only); an item in the control account but not in the individual account, or the other way round; different amounts in the two; returns not posted to the individual account; discount recorded in one place only; bad debts written off in one place only; a contra recorded in one place only; a dishonoured cheque reinstated in one place only; and a double posting.

Debtors at 1 March ₦150,000; credit sales ₦320,000; cash sales ₦180,000; cash received from debtors ₦280,000; returns inwards ₦18,000; discount allowed ₦15,000; bad debts ₦10,000; dishonoured cheque ₦8,000; interest ₦3,000; contra ₦6,000. The individual debtors total ₦152,000.

Debit side: 150,000 + 320,000 + 8,000 + 3,000 = ₦481,000. Credit side: 280,000 + 18,000 + 15,000 + 10,000 + 6,000 = ₦329,000. Closing balance ₦152,000, which equals the individual total. The reconciliation shows no difference.

title: Purchases Ledger Control Account
summary: The purchases ledger (total creditors) control account: its structure, items and worked examples.

p: The purchases ledger control account shows the total of all the individual creditors' accounts in the purchases ledger. It is also called the total creditors account, the creditors control account, the payables control account or the bought ledger control account. It helps management, helps to find errors and acts as an internal check, just as the sales ledger control account does.

The sales ledger control account shows what customers owe us (an asset). The purchases ledger control account shows what we owe suppliers (a liability). They follow the same ideas but with opposite sides.
Creditors are liabilities, so the account has a credit balance. Credit side: things that INCREASE what we owe. Debit side: things that DECREASE it.

head: Debit side (decreases creditors)
Credit side (increases creditors)
rows: Cash and bank paid to creditors
Dishonoured cheque (our cheque to a supplier)
Closing balance c/d (creditors at the end)

p: Credit purchases are only purchases on credit, from the purchases day book; cash purchases are not included because they do not create creditors. A dishonoured cheque issued by us puts the debt back, so we still owe the supplier. Interest charged by suppliers (for late payment) also increases the debt. Cash paid, returns outwards, discount received and the contra reduce the debt.
Creditors at 1 February ₦60,000; credit purchases ₦180,000; cash paid to creditors ₦150,000; returns outwards ₦12,000; discount received ₦8,000.

Creditors at 1 May ₦100,000; credit purchases ₦250,000; cash purchases ₦90,000; cash paid to creditors ₦210,000; cheques paid ₦40,000; returns outwards ₦18,000; discount received ₦15,000; interest charged by suppliers ₦3,000; our dishonoured cheque ₦6,000; contra with debtors ₦5,000.

Cash purchases of ₦90,000 are left out. Cash and cheques paid reduce creditors and are shown as one figure. The dishonoured cheque and the interest are credits because they increase what we owe. The contra is a debit because it reduces what we owe. The ₦71,000 is the total owed to all suppliers at 31 May.

title: Contra Entries, Comparison and Reconciliation of Control Accounts
summary: How a contra entry is made, a comparison of the sales and purchases control accounts, reconciling the creditors, and practice with answers.

p: A contra is made when the same person is both a debtor and a creditor. Example: Tunde Limited owes us ₦15,000 (a debtor) and we owe Tunde Limited ₦10,000 (a creditor). We agree to set off ₦10,000.
Journal: Dr Purchases ledger control account ₦10,000; Cr Sales ledger control account ₦10,000 (being a contra entry for set-off).

Effect: in the sales ledger control account, ₦10,000 appears on the credit side (debtors fall from ₦15,000 to ₦5,000). In the purchases ledger control account, ₦10,000 appears on the debit side (creditors fall from ₦10,000 to nil). The same amount appears in both control accounts, on opposite sides. After the contra, Tunde owes us ₦5,000 net and we owe him nothing.

p: Both are control accounts that summarise individual accounts. Both help to find errors and save time. Both are used for reconciliation. They have similar items, on opposite sides.
Compare the control account balance with the total of the individual creditors' balances.
Example: control ₦71,000. Suppliers: A 28,000; B 20,000; C 15,000; D 8,000 = ₦71,000. They agree.

Example with an error: control ₦71,000; individual total ₦68,000; difference ₦3,000. Cause: a discount received of ₦3,000 was recorded in the control account but not in the individual creditor's account. Record it there and the total becomes ₦71,000.

title: Depreciation: Meaning, Causes and Reasons
summary: What depreciation is, which assets depreciate, seven causes and seven reasons for providing for it, and the main methods.

p: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life. It is also the fall in value of a fixed asset because of use, the passage of time or obsolescence.

Key points: it applies to fixed assets only, not to current assets; it is a non-cash expense (no money is paid out); it is an estimate; it reduces the value of the asset in the balance sheet; it is charged as an expense in the profit and loss account; and it matches cost with income (the accrual concept).

Assets that depreciate: buildings, machinery, motor vehicles, furniture, equipment, computers and tools. Assets that normally do not: land (it usually keeps or gains value), stock (it is treated differently), investments and antiques.

1. Wear and tear: normal use damages the asset (an engine wears out; furniture is scratched). 2. Obsolescence: new technology makes an asset out of date even though it still works (an old computer replaced by a faster one). 3. Passage of time: assets lose value with age even if not used (rubber perishes, paint fades). 4. Depletion: the quantity of a natural resource falls as it is extracted (a mine, an oil well, a quarry). 5. Effluxion of time: rights that last for a fixed period expire (a 10-year lease, a patent, a licence). 6. Inadequacy: the asset becomes too small for a growing business. 7. Accidents and damage: a vehicle crash, fire damage.

1. To apply the accrual concept: a machine that costs ₦100,000 and lasts 10 years is charged ₦10,000 a year, not ₦100,000 in year one. 2. To show the true profit: without depreciation the profit is overstated (₦50,000 instead of a truer ₦40,000). 3. To show a realistic asset value in the balance sheet. 4. To provide for replacement: keeping back profit each year helps the business to have funds to buy a new asset (note that depreciation itself does not create cash; the profit must actually be saved). 5. To follow the law and accounting standards. 6. To calculate the correct capital. 7. For tax: capital allowances reduce taxable profit.

The main methods are the straight-line method (equal instalment) and the reducing balance method (diminishing balance). Others are the revaluation method (used for small tools and livestock), the depletion method (mines and quarries), the machine hour or units of production method (based on use), the sum of years' digits method and the annuity method. In SS1 you study the first two.

title: The Straight-Line Method of Depreciation
summary: The formula, advantages and disadvantages of the straight-line method, three worked examples including part-year purchase, and how to record depreciation using a provision account.

p: In the straight-line method an equal amount of depreciation is charged each year over the life of the asset. It is also called the fixed instalment or equal instalment method.

Annual depreciation = (cost − scrap value) ÷ useful life. Or annual depreciation = cost × rate %. Cost is the purchase price. Scrap (residual or salvage) value is the amount the asset is expected to fetch at the end of its life. Useful life is the estimated number of years of use.

Advantages: simple and easy; the same charge each year; suits assets with steady use; easy to predict. Disadvantages: it ignores the pattern of use; it assumes equal benefit each year; it may not match actual wear; and repair costs usually rise with age, so the total cost is not even. It suits buildings, furniture, leases, patents and copyrights.

sections.h: Example 1: using cost, scrap value and life
p: Machine cost ₦100,000; scrap value ₦10,000; life 10 years. Annual depreciation = (100,000 − 10,000) ÷ 10 = ₦9,000 a year.

A vehicle costs ₦500,000 and is depreciated at 20% a year (straight line). Annual depreciation = 500,000 × 20% = ₦100,000. After 5 years the total depreciation is ₦500,000, so the net book value is nil.

Furniture is bought on 1 April 2024 for ₦60,000 and is depreciated at 10% a year. Accounts close on 31 December. Full-year depreciation is 60,000 × 10% = ₦6,000. It was held for 9 months. Depreciation for 2024 = 6,000 × 9/12 = ₦4,500. Formula: cost × rate × (months held ÷ 12).

Keep the asset at cost. Each year: Dr Depreciation account (expense) ₦9,000; Cr Provision for depreciation account ₦9,000. The depreciation account is closed to the profit and loss account. The provision account collects the amounts year by year: ₦9,000 at the end of year 1, ₦18,000 at the end of year 2. The balance sheet shows the machinery at cost ₦100,000, less provision ₦9,000 (year 1) or ₦18,000 (year 2), giving net book value ₦91,000 or ₦82,000.
Advantages of the provision method: it shows the original cost, the total depreciation to date and the net book value.

title: The Reducing Balance Method of Depreciation
summary: How depreciation is calculated on the reducing book value, the pattern it follows, worked examples including part-year purchase, and how it appears in the accounts.

p: In the reducing balance method (also called diminishing balance or written-down value method), depreciation is calculated each year on the net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation), not on the cost. Year 1: cost × rate. Year 2: (cost − year 1 depreciation) × rate. Each year: opening net book value × rate.

Features: the charge falls each year; it is highest in the early years; it never reaches zero, since a percentage of what remains always leaves something behind (₦100 × 20% = ₦20 leaves ₦80; ₦80 × 20% = ₦16 leaves ₦64; and so on).
A motor vehicle costs ₦500,000 and is depreciated at 25% a year on the reducing balance.
Machinery bought on 1 January 2021 for ₦200,000. Depreciation is 30% a year on the reducing balance. Find the charge for each year and show the machinery in the balance sheet at 31 December 2024.

The machinery account stays at the cost of ₦200,000 every year. The provision for depreciation account is credited each year with the year's charge and the balance builds up: ₦60,000, ₦102,000, ₦131,400, ₦151,980. Each year the journal is Dr Depreciation, Cr Provision for depreciation. Balance sheet at 31 December 2024: machinery at cost ₦200,000, less provision for depreciation ₦151,980, net book value ₦48,020.

An asset is bought on 1 July 2024 for ₦120,000 and depreciated at 20% on the reducing balance. The year ends on 31 December. Full year = 120,000 × 20% = ₦24,000. For 6 months = 24,000 × 6/12 = ₦12,000. Net book value at 31 December 2024 = ₦108,000.
In 2025 the year is a full year: opening NBV ₦108,000 × 20% = ₦21,600, so closing NBV is ₦86,400. After the first part year, each following year is a full year on the reducing balance.
Equipment bought on 1 January 2022 for ₦80,000 at 25% reducing balance: 2022 ₦20,000 (NBV ₦60,000); 2023 ₦15,000 (NBV ₦45,000); 2024 ₦11,250 (NBV ₦33,750).

sections.h: Advantages and disadvantages of reducing balance
p: Advantages: the pattern is realistic (an asset loses most value early); costs are matched with income (a new asset has a high depreciation charge and low repairs, an old asset has a low charge and high repairs, so the total yearly cost is more even); it gives tax advantages by deferring tax; it writes off the asset faster, which suits assets that quickly become out of date; and it is cautious (prudent).

Disadvantages: the calculation is more involved; the asset never reaches zero and may not match the true scrap value; profit is higher in later years, which makes comparisons harder; and the right rate is hard to find.

Use the straight-line method for buildings, furniture, leases, patents and copyrights, and for assets with steady use and a known life (for example, a ₦10 million building over 50 years is ₦200,000 a year). Use reducing balance for motor vehicles, computers, phones and other technology, and for machinery with fast obsolescence or heavy use in the early years.
Think about the pattern of use, the rate of obsolescence, repair costs (rising with age favours reducing balance), what management prefers and the type of asset.

An asset costing ₦200,000 depreciated at 20% for 5 years. Straight line: ₦40,000 a year, total ₦200,000, nil value. Reducing balance: ₦40,000; ₦32,000; ₦25,600; ₦20,480; ₦16,384, total ₦134,464, leaving a net book value of ₦65,536.

Equipment costing ₦300,000 for 4 years at 20%: straight line ₦60,000 a year, total ₦240,000, net book value ₦60,000. Reducing balance: ₦60,000; ₦48,000; ₦38,400; ₦30,720, total ₦177,120, net book value ₦122,880.
